Se valoran especialmente los conocimientos de Python, imágenes satelitales o conjuntos de datos científicos.

Buscamos a alguien con curiosidad, capacidad de trabajar en equipo y disposición para aprender.
summary:
ARES-MIV is a web-based 3D Mars exploration and route-planning prototype developed for NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. Focused on Gale Crater and Mount Sharp, it combines an interactive Mars globe with geospatial tools to support preliminary exploration planning.

Users can explore Mars using CesiumJS, switch between MOLA topographic relief and Viking MDIM 2.1 imagery, and select origin and destination coordinates. Its Python FastAPI backend uses an A* algorithm and a 5-meter slope GeoTIFF derived from Gale Crater elevation data to calculate potential astronaut walking routes based on terrain slope and traversal costs. The API provides route geometry, distance, maximum slope, estimated walking time, rest periods, and suggested stops.

The project integrates NASA planetary data and technologies including Vue 3, CesiumJS, Python, FastAPI, Rasterio, NumPy, Docker, AWS S3, and Render. Rover routing is implemented as a separate frontend simulation.

ARES-MIV demonstrates how planetary datasets and geospatial algorithms can support Martian terrain exploration. It is an experimental prototype with simplified walking assumptions, not certified mission navigation software.
details:
Project Overview

ARES-MIV is an interactive 3D geospatial exploration and route-planning prototype developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge "Interplanetary Survival Guide: Martian Map". It focuses on Gale Crater, particularly the Mount Sharp region, and explores how planetary data can support preliminary astronaut exploration planning.

How It Works

The frontend is built with Vue 3 and CesiumJS. It provides an interactive Mars globe where users can explore the study area, switch between MOLA topographic relief and Viking MDIM 2.1 imagery, and select origin and destination coordinates.

The Python FastAPI backend processes a 5-meter slope GeoTIFF derived from Gale Crater elevation data. It uses the A* pathfinding algorithm to calculate potential astronaut walking routes based on terrain slope constraints and traversal costs. The API returns route geometry, distance, maximum slope, estimated walking time, rest periods, and suggested stops.

Geospatial data is stored and retrieved through AWS S3, allowing the backend to access the required terrain files. Docker is used for containerization, and the API is deployed on Render.

Rover routing is implemented separately as a frontend simulation and is not calculated by the backend's A* walking-route planner.

Data and Technologies

The project uses NASA planetary resources, including MOLA topographic data and Viking MDIM 2.1 imagery, alongside Gale Crater elevation data. Its technology stack includes Vue 3, JavaScript, CesiumJS, Python, FastAPI, Rasterio, NumPy, Docker, AWS S3, and Render.

Innovation and Intended Impact

ARES-MIV brings planetary visualization, geospatial processing, and terrain-aware pathfinding into one application. Instead of treating Martian terrain as a simple map, it considers slope and traversal costs when proposing potential walking routes. This demonstrates how publicly available planetary datasets can be transformed into interactive tools for understanding terrain and exploring possible routes.

Use of Artificial Intelligence

Generative AI tools, including GPT, were used to accelerate parts of the software development process, particularly coding assistance, debugging, and documentation formatting. The team wrote the instructions and requirements used to guide these tools, with GPT also assisting in organizing and formatting Markdown documentation. The team reviewed, adapted, and tested the resulting code and documentation and remains responsible for the final implementation.

Limitations

ARES-MIV is an experimental prototype. Walking speed, rest periods, and terrain constraints rely on simplified assumptions and have not been validated for real astronaut operations. The project does not implement radiation-dose calculations or provide certified mission navigation. Rover routing is a separate frontend simulation.
